pages.name: Space Travel
pages.html:
Space Travel

Space Travel: Interstellar space travel is tracked on a hex map, where each hex represents a parsec of space.

  • Subsector map: Each subsector map is a 8 x 10 parsec hex area, where each hex is numbered. Subsectors are considered “local” regions within an interstellar society.
  • Sector map: A sector map is made up of 16 subsector maps and represents a significant portion of space.
  • Capital World: each subsector will have a capital world which is determined by the planet with the highest population and tech level, or as the referee determines for the campaign. If an interstellar society has many worlds and expands past the boundaries of a subsector map, then the referee can choose one of the subsector capitals as the primary capital for that society, with the other capital worlds being local ancillary capitals.
  • Courier Routes: All subsector maps will have main courier routes between planets with Population code of 6+. The referee should map those routes when constructing a subsector map. Routes do not need to be mapped out between adjacent parsec hexes. Worlds with population codes of 5 or less will depend on freelance couriers to provide courier services.

Book p.88

pages.name: Space Exploration and World Encounters
pages.html:
Space Exploration and World Encounters

Space Exploration and World Encounters: Roll 1D when jumping to an unmapped parsec hex on a subsector map.

  • Inhabited system encounter: Result of 4+
  • Empty: Result of 1-3
  • Uninhabited star system: 0 or less

Sector Density Modifications: Use the following dice modifiers to the above 1D roll based on the assumed density of celestial bodies in each subsector of space the spacer is passing through when entering a parsec hex:

  • Rift or assumed empty sectors: -2DM
  • Sparse sectors: -1DM
  • Typical density sectors: +0DM
  • Densely populated sectors: +1DM

Book p.88

pages.name: Uninhabited Star Systems
pages.html:
Uninhabited Star Systems

Uninhabited star system: There are many star systems within parsecs of each other, but only the ones capable of maintaining life will be considered inhabited. Those that are encountered that are uninhabitable are unstable red dwarf stars that have frequent flares, which make them dangerous for long-term habitation but are too dim to easily see from parsecs away. These systems could be used for adventures if the referee wishes, but assume that those systems mostly have barren worlds and asteroids.

When an inhabited system is encountered, generate the star system and the main world.

Book p.88

pages.name: Star System Details
pages.html:
Star System Details

Star System Details: Use the following to determine the details of the star system a main world is located in.

Star systems are identified by the parsec hex number on the subsector map, the star type, the number of stellar objects, the number of how many stellar objects are inhabited, and how many gas giants are in the system.

  • Example; Chadwick System: 0205-G521. Chadwick is found on hex 0101 of the subsector star map, has a yellow sun, five planets,—two of which are occupied—and one gas giant.

Book p.88

pages.name: Primary Stars
pages.html:
Primary Stars

Primary Star: Use the following to determine the star of the system.

  • Star type: When determining the Star type, roll 2D and add the Sector Density DM.
  • Habitable Zone (HZ): Otherwise known as the “Goldilocks zone,” this will be the location of the main world within this system. Any other inhabited planets will have to be within +/- 25% of this range, for living on the surface. Any settlements outside of this zone require being underground or within a shielded and insulated controlled environment. Planets within the Goldilocks zone are capable of life and terraforming.
  • Number of other stellar objects: Roll on this column to determine the number of other stellar objects in the system. This usually represents planets or planetoids but may also include asteroid belts.
    • Mass (M): 1M equals the mass of Earth’s Sun.
    • Radius (R): 1 radius equals the radius of Earth’s Sun.
    • Astronomical Unit: 1 AU equals 1.5 million kilometres. This is roughly the distance of the Earth from the Sun.

pages.name: Other Stellar Objects
pages.html:
Other Stellar Objects

Other Stellar Objects: For every generated planet, roll 2D.

2DObject Types
2Unique Celestial Observation: Use the Unique Celestial Observation table to determine what type is found within this star system.
3-5Barren: Rock ball, devoid of atmosphere. May have industrial facilities or small colonies. Barren planets will have D3 moons.
6-8Gas Giant: Gas giants will have 1D moons around them. These moons may function as bases for pirates, corporations, or other groups who use the gas giant as a source of revenue or ambushes.
9-11Structure: This represents notable or important man- or sophont-made structures. Roll 1D
1) Belter base
2) Communication or remote research station
3) Remote starbase port station
4) Scrap or salvage base
5) Colony cluster: 1D colonies
6) Abandoned structure with a 50% chance of being occupied by squatters, pirates, or other spacers. Roll D3 on this list to determine the type of abandoned structure.
12Secondary World: An inhabited world, a minor planet to the main world in the star system.

Moons: To determine the size of each moon, roll a D3-1 per moon on Step 1 of the World generator.

Book p.89

pages.name: Unique Celestial Observations
pages.html:
Unique Celestial Observation Table

2DUnique TypeDescription
2AnomalyA strange artificial celestial body exists within the system either as a stellar object/event or as a planetside anomaly. See the Anomalies Table to determine what type is observed.
3-4Shattered WorldA planet or planetoid that has been hit by another celestial body, shattering it in many large pieces. This world still has its normal orbit but is a hazard because of the debris that is slingshot from its fractured form. Pilot checks incur -1DM while moving through this system.
5-9ClusterA massive cloud of asteroids or planetoids made of minerals and ice clutter a large portion of the system, making travel difficult, providing -2DM to pilot checks and -1DM to Astrogation. Roll D3 to determine the cluster’s shape: 1) Torus 2) spherical 3) asymmetrical
10-11Secondary StarThere is a secondary star that is twice as weak as the primary star. Jumping is -2DM.
12+Black HoleThere is a black hole that is the primary gravitational body, but the sun and planets exist outside of the Schwartzchild radius of the black hole, allowing for the planets and star to not be pulled in. Jumping in and out of this system is -3DM.
